description: Sanctity of life and Pikuach Nefesh; soul and body; resurrection, Sheol, Gan Eden and Gehenna.
content_html:
The Sanctity of Human Life

One of the most fundamental principles in Jewish ethics is the sanctity of life. Judaism teaches that human life has unique and irreplaceable value because every person is created in the image of G-d (tzelem Elohim). Genesis 1:27 states: “G-d created mankind in his own image, in the image of G-d he created them; male and female he created them.” This verse grounds the sanctity of all human life: every person, regardless of age, ability or status, bears the divine image and deserves protection and dignity.

The sanctity of life is also underpinned by the creation account in Genesis 2:7: “The Lord G-d formed a man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being.” The image of G-d breathing life directly into a human being conveys the intimate, sacred nature of each human life. The sixth commandment, “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13), makes the protection of human life a divine obligation.

Key Fact

The sanctity of life in Judaism is rooted in two key teachings: Genesis 1:27 (humans are created in G-d’s image, giving every person intrinsic dignity) and Genesis 2:7 (G-d breathed life into humanity, making life sacred). The commandment “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13) reinforces this by making the protection of life a direct divine command.

Pikuach Nefesh and the Sanctity of Life

Pikuach Nefesh (literally “watching over a soul”) is the practical application of the sanctity of life to Jewish law. Because life is so sacred, the Talmud teaches that almost every other Mitzvah must be set aside to preserve it. Leviticus 19:16 (“do not stand idly by the blood of your neighbour”) is cited as a source for the duty to intervene when someone’s life is at risk.

Pikuach Nefesh affects Jewish life in concrete ways. A Jewish doctor must treat patients on Shabbat or Jewish festivals if their lives are at risk. A sick person may eat non-kosher food if it is medically necessary. Communities must fund emergency services. The principle extends beyond individual acts: Jewish communities are obligated to support medical care, welfare services and any institution that protects life.

A significant debate in Jewish ethics concerns whether Pikuach Nefesh extends to relieving severe suffering even at the cost of shortening life. Orthodox Jewish authorities generally hold that Pikuach Nefesh protects and extends life; actively shortening life, even to end suffering, goes against the principle. Most Orthodox rulings therefore oppose active euthanasia.

Progressive (Reform) Jewish thinkers have sometimes argued that quality of life and the relief of suffering are also Jewish values, and that in some circumstances allowing a person to die (passive euthanasia) or relieving pain even at some cost to life’s length may be consistent with Jewish ethics. The distinction between human and non-human life is also debated: some authorities extend the principle of Pikuach Nefesh only to human beings, citing the unique status of humans created in G-d’s image; others argue it should inform attitudes to all sentient life.

Soul and Body in Jewish Belief

Judaism teaches that a human being is a unity of soul and body. Genesis 2:7 is read as describing the creation of this unity: the physical body (basar) formed from dust, animated by G-d’s own breath (neshama — the soul or spirit). The soul is the divine element within each person; the body is its earthly dwelling. This understanding of human nature shapes Jewish attitudes to life, death and what follows death.

Unlike some other traditions, classical Judaism has generally resisted the idea that the body is merely a prison from which the soul escapes at death. Rather, the bodily dimension of human life is valued and respected: Jewish burial practice, for instance, emphasises the dignity of the body. The belief that G-d will ultimately restore the whole person — body and soul — shapes traditional Jewish ideas about resurrection.

Life After Death: Key Concepts

Jewish beliefs about life after death are varied and have developed over centuries. Several concepts are important:

Sheol is the term used in the Hebrew Bible for the realm of the dead. In earlier Jewish thought, Sheol was simply where all people went after death — a shadowy, diminished state rather than a place of reward or punishment. It was not heaven or hell in the later sense.

Gan Eden (literally “the Garden of Eden”) is the term used in Jewish tradition for the paradise where the souls of the righteous enjoy G-d’s presence after death. It is understood as a state of spiritual bliss and closeness to G-d, rather than necessarily a physical garden.

Gehenna is understood in Jewish thought as a place of purification or punishment for souls who require correction after death. Importantly, in most Jewish traditions Gehenna is not seen as eternal: the maximum time a soul spends there is twelve months, after which it is either purified and enters Gan Eden or, in extreme cases, ceases to exist. This is different from the Christian concept of permanent hell.

Key Fact

Three key afterlife concepts in Judaism: Sheol — the shadowy realm of the dead in the Hebrew Bible; Gan Eden — paradise where righteous souls rest in G-d’s presence; Gehenna — a place of purification (not usually eternal), after which souls are cleansed and may enter Gan Eden. Daniel 12:2–3 is the clearest Hebrew Bible reference to resurrection and different destinations for the righteous and the wicked.

Resurrection and Judgement

The concept of Resurrection — that the dead will be physically raised at the end of time — appears most clearly in the Hebrew Bible in Daniel 12:2–3: “Multitudes who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake: some to everlasting life, others to shame and everlasting contempt. Those who are wise will shine like the brightness of the heavens.” This passage teaches that there will be a future resurrection in which the righteous and the wicked receive different outcomes.

Judgement by G-d is a key aspect of Jewish afterlife belief. The Rosh Hashannah and Yom Kippur period focuses intensely on this theme — Jews examine their actions over the past year and seek forgiveness, with the belief that G-d inscribes their fate in the Book of Life. However, Jewish views on the exact nature and timing of judgement vary: some emphasise judgement at death; others emphasise a final judgement at the end of time.

Belief in the resurrection of the body is a central doctrine of Orthodox Judaism, listed among the thirteen principles of faith compiled by Maimonides. In this view, at the end of time G-d will restore the dead bodily, and the righteous will enjoy the World to Come (Olam Ha-Ba). The resurrection is understood as a physical event, consistent with the Jewish valuation of bodily life as God-given.

Progressive (Reform) Judaism has often moved away from a literal belief in bodily resurrection, focusing instead on the immortality of the soul — the idea that the spiritual dimension of a person continues after death in the presence of G-d. Some Reform Jews interpret afterlife language metaphorically, understanding “life after death” as the continuing influence a person has through their actions and legacy. Conservative (Masorti) Jews generally retain the traditional language of resurrection but allow a range of interpretations regarding its literal or symbolic meaning.
exam_tip_html: For ‘Explain’ questions on the Jewish afterlife, be specific: use and explain the terms Sheol, Gan Eden and Gehenna rather than generic phrases like ‘heaven and hell.’ A common error is to say Gehenna is eternal punishment like the Christian hell — clarify that in most Jewish thought it is a temporary, purifying state (usually no more than twelve months). For questions on the sanctity of life, always link Pikuach Nefesh back to its scriptural basis (Genesis 1:27; Leviticus 19:16). For 15-mark ‘Discuss’ questions, compare Orthodox (bodily resurrection, all 613 Mitzvot binding) with Progressive (immortality of soul, greater emphasis on quality of life) views and reach a justified conclusion. Accurate spelling of ‘Pikuach Nefesh,’ ‘Gehenna,’ ‘Gan Eden’ and ‘resurrection’ is rewarded.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The sanctity of life is rooted in Genesis 1:27 (humans created in G-d’s image) and Genesis 2:7 (G-d’s breath gives life). Pikuach Nefesh means preserving life overrides nearly all other Mitzvot; Leviticus 19:16 forbids standing by while another’s life is at risk.
  • Judaism understands humans as a unity of soul and body. The key afterlife concepts are Sheol (shadowy realm of the dead in the Hebrew Bible), Gan Eden (paradise for the righteous) and Gehenna (temporary purification, usually no more than twelve months).
  • Daniel 12:2–3 provides the clearest Hebrew Bible reference to resurrection and different destinations for the righteous and the wicked. Orthodox Jews affirm bodily resurrection; Progressive Jews often focus on the soul’s immortality or interpret afterlife language metaphorically.

practice_questions.text: Describe what Jews believe about the relationship between the soul and the body.
practice_questions.marks: Judaism teaches that a human being is a unity of soul and body [1 mark]; the soul (neshama) is the divine element given by G-d at creation (Genesis 2:7 — G-d breathed life into humanity), while the body is its earthly dwelling, both of which are valued and respected [1 mark]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Outline what Jews believe about life after death, referring to Sheol, Gan Eden and Gehenna.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: Sheol is the shadowy realm of the dead in the Hebrew Bible, understood as a diminished state rather than reward or punishment (1 mark); Gan Eden is paradise where the souls of the righteous rest in G-d’s presence after death (1 mark); Gehenna is a place of purification for souls, generally not permanent — most Jewish traditions say souls remain there no more than twelve months (1 mark); Daniel 12:2–3 describes a future resurrection and different destinies for the righteous and the wicked (1 mark). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two Jewish teachings about the sanctity of life.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• All humans are created in the image of G-d (Genesis 1:27 — tzelem Elohim): this gives every person intrinsic worth and dignity, regardless of age, ability or status. This means human life cannot be treated as expendable.
• G-d breathed life directly into humanity (Genesis 2:7): life is a divine gift and therefore belongs ultimately to G-d, not to humans. This shapes Jewish opposition to taking life without divine sanction.
• The commandment “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13) makes the protection of life a direct divine obligation.
• Pikuach Nefesh (Leviticus 19:16) — the duty to preserve life — overrides almost all other Mitzvot, showing how highly Judaism values life: saving a life on Shabbat, for example, is not just permitted but required.
[6 marks: up to 3 marks per teaching — 1 for naming, 2 for explaining, 3 for developing with a source]

practice_questions.text: 'Jewish beliefs about life after death are less important than Jewish beliefs about how to live in this world.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Judaism is often described as a ‘this-world’ religion: the Torah is primarily concerned with how Jews live in the present — keeping the Mitzvot, building a just society, observing the covenant.
• The 613 Mitzvot deal overwhelmingly with life in this world; Jewish law (‘halachah’) is a detailed guide to living, not primarily a preparation for death.
• Deuteronomy 30:19 (“choose life”) focuses on present choices; Pikuach Nefesh prioritises life in this world above ritual observance.
• Progressive (Reform) Jews often interpret afterlife language metaphorically, suggesting that what matters is living according to Jewish values now.

Arguments against:
• Orthodox Judaism includes belief in bodily resurrection (tekhiyat ha-metim) as one of Maimonides’ thirteen principles of faith — it is a core doctrinal belief, not optional.
• The themes of Rosh Hashannah and Yom Kippur — G-d’s judgement, the Book of Life — show that life after death is deeply embedded in Jewish prayer and community life.
• Daniel 12:2–3 gives clear scriptural basis for resurrection and future judgement, showing that afterlife belief is not peripheral but rooted in scripture.
• The hope of Gan Eden (paradise) gives meaning and comfort to Jews facing suffering, persecution or death — as evidenced throughout Jewish history.

Mastering: Both sides fully developed with named sources (Deuteronomy 30:19; Daniel 12:2–3; Genesis 1:27; Maimonides’ principles), explicit weighing, justified conclusion that may acknowledge the balance between this-worldly ethics and afterlife belief in Judaism.
Secure: Clear two-sided argument with some source reference; reasoned conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger; limited source reference; simple conclusion.
Emerging: Only one perspective; no sources; minimal conclusion.
[15 marks — SPaG assessed on this response]

practice_questions.text: Outline how Jewish views on resurrection and the afterlife differ between Orthodox and Progressive communities.
practice_questions.marks: Any three from: Orthodox Judaism affirms bodily resurrection (tekhiyat ha-metim) as a core belief, listed in Maimonides’ thirteen principles (1 mark); at the end of time, the dead will be physically raised and face G-d’s judgement (1 mark); Progressive Jews often focus on the immortality of the soul rather than bodily resurrection (1 mark); some Progressive Jews interpret afterlife language metaphorically — meaning a person’s influence and legacy live on (1 mark); Conservative Jews generally retain traditional language but allow a range of interpretations (1 mark). [3 marks]

glossary_terms.definition: The belief that human life is sacred, precious and G-d-given, and therefore must be protected and respected.
The Jewish principle that the duty to save or preserve human life overrides almost all other commandments in the Torah.
The immaterial, spiritual dimension of a person, understood in Judaism as the breath of life given by G-d, distinct from the physical body.
In the Hebrew Bible, the shadowy realm of the dead; the place all people go after death, understood as a state of diminished existence rather than punishment or reward.
Hebrew for 'Garden of Eden'; in Jewish belief, the paradise where righteous souls rest after death.
In Jewish belief, a place of purification or punishment for souls after death; not necessarily permanent, and often compared to purgatory in Christian thought.
The belief that, at the end of time, the dead will be restored to bodily life and face G-d's judgement.
The evaluation by G-d of each person's deeds, determining their fate after death; a central concept in Jewish eschatology.
